name: FPC (Fast Prefix Coder)
baseline: zlib Huffman (zlibh) and FSE Huff0 (fsehuf) as packaged in TurboBench
workload: Order-0 entropy coding of silesia.tar (211 MB) on a Core i5-4460 and of enwik8 on an Orange Pi PC Plus (Allwinner H3), run through TurboBench.
claimed_speedup: silesia.tar: fpc 32 decodes at 897.28 MB/s versus 715.36 MB/s for fsehuf, 591.30 MB/s for rans_static16, 483.55 MB/s for fse and 243.08 MB/s for zlibh (about 1.25x fsehuf and 3.7x zlibh, derived from page data); fpc 16 compresses at 476.96 MB/s versus 248.55 MB/s for zlibh. Ratios are within 0.1 percentage points of the others (61.4% for fpc 32 and fsehuf). On the H3 board enwik8, fpc 32 decodes at 90.70 MB/s versus 61.11 MB/s for fsehuf.
hardware: Intel Core i5-4460 @ 3.20GHz (silesia.tar); Orange Pi PC Plus, Allwinner H3 (enwik8)
tradeoffs: Prefix (Huffman) coder with length-limited package-merge codes (default max 11 bits), 3 interleaved streams by default, adaptive block subdivision. Static per block, so it cannot reach the ratio of adaptive arithmetic coders such as fpaq0p_sh (58.7% on silesia.tar).
caveats: Numbers were produced with the TurboBench harness but by the project author, and the README lists no compiler or flags, so this is B rather than A. fsehuf compresses faster than fpc 32 (574.79 versus 548.16 MB/s), so the win is decode speed. Last commit was April 2022. The older owner name algorithm314/FPC redirects to kagiannis/FPC (observed while fetching).

name: zune-entropy
baseline: FSE library (Huff0 Huffman and FSE tANS modes), Yann Collet's FiniteStateEntropy
workload: Order-0 Huffman and tANS encode and decode of enwik8 on an AMD Ryzen 5 4500U, compared with FSE/Huff0 and FSE/TANS.
claimed_speedup: enwik8 Huffman: 940.97 MB/s encode and 1310.28 MB/s decode versus FSE/Huff0 at 924.6 and 1049.5 MB/s. tANS: 602.56 MB/s encode and 1022.93 MB/s decode versus FSE/TANS at 457.7 and 572.8 MB/s. README says the tANS is faster because it interleaves more.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 4500U with Radeon Graphics, 6 cores, 8 MiB L3
tradeoffs: Worse compression ratio than FSE on the same file: Huffman 65.00% versus 63.26%, tANS 63.90% versus 63.12%. The README says the Huffman part is a simple illustration. Rust only; no C API.
caveats: First-party numbers on one file; the benchmark driver lives in a separate repo (etemesi254/zcif_bin) that was not opened. No compiler flags stated. The repo is declared beta and some files (silesia/mozilla) do not work. No LICENSE file found (raw fetch of LICENSE, LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE returned 404), so the code is reference only. Cargo.toml does not name a license.

name: RGC (Recursive Group Coding)
baseline: static 8-bit arithmetic coder (AC); TurboRC rcc2senc() range coder also listed
workload: Entropy coding of tst.dat, 1 MB of quantized DCT coefficients from 32x32 image blocks (rgc_demo.c); the headline result is compression ratio on large alphabets.
claimed_speedup: README: 'running about twice as fast as the simplest static 8-bit AC' and 'about twice as fast as a range coder' with moderate optimization. Table on tst.dat: RGC 224,071 bytes in 0.01 s versus TurboRC rcc2senc() 237,380 bytes in 0.03 s (3x faster, derived from page data), versus AC 8-bit 261,695 bytes with no time given.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 'cl /O2 /MD rgc_demo.c' shown as the build example, not stated as the benchmark build
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; also on PyPI as rgclib
tradeoffs: Two-file C library (rgc.c, rgc.h) plus Python wrapper. Needs statistically homogeneous data; loses to AC by about 1-2% on random 8-bit data and is unsuited to files of a few kilobytes because group symbol lists dominate. Targets large alphabets (up to 1024-byte symbols).
caveats: The speed claim is a prose statement; the only timing table is a single 1 MB file with no CPU, no repeat count and no AC time. Most of the table is compression ratio, not speed. The AC 8-bit baseline is not a named library. The 2009 paper (Telecommunications and Radio Engineering) is checked into the repo but was not opened. Author-run, so C.

name: constriction
baseline: arithmetic coding as implemented in the arcode crate (cgbur/arcode-rs)
workload: Encode and decode of 3-million-symbol i.i.d. messages spanning 0.001 to 10 bits per symbol, from a real-world application, aggregated over all messages.
claimed_speedup: Default ANS (24/32/64): 24.2 ns/symbol encode and 6.1 ns/symbol decode with 0.0015% bit-rate overhead. Default range coder (24/32/64): 16.6 / 14.3 ns/symbol with 0.0237% overhead. arcode arithmetic coding baseline: 43.2 / 85.6 ns/symbol with 0.0004% overhead. About 14x faster decode for ANS and 6x for RC, and 1.8x and 2.6x faster encode (all derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Rust release mode (cargo bench); toolchain version 1.75 or later required; exact rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated
tradeoffs: Rust library with Python bindings; no C or C++ API, so use from C++ needs an FFI wrapper. ANS is last-in-first-out (suits bits-back coding), RC is first-in-first-out. Models are user-supplied (probability tables), so this measures the coder core, not a full compressor. Small-precision presets trade 4% bit-rate overhead for speed.
caveats: Methodology is in Section 5.2 of arXiv:2201.01741 and the benchmark code is in github.com/bamler-lab/understanding-ans (BSL-1.0, benchmarks subdirectory); arXiv was blocked here so the paper was not opened and the repo's CPU and flags were not confirmed beyond the README. Baseline is a Rust arithmetic coder, not Huffman, rANS or Huff0 and nothing C or C++. Not compared against FSE, Huff0 or ryg_rans. Peer-review status of the paper not verified, so B is by the public-benchmark-code route short of A (rustc version missing).
